text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- EU finance ministers approve German convergence programme. Finance Minister Theo Waigel is stunned by speculation
- Krupp wants to takeover Thyssen, Thyssen feels threatened. Fears about job losses. Majority stake in Thyssen would cost more than five billion marks
- The comments by countless politicians about European monetary union lead to uncertainty in the financial markets
- Government wants to reduce wind energy subsidies
- Bank association says no tax increases for the euro
HANDELSBLATT
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says Maastricht criteria will be fulfilled by Germany. A delay in EMU remains taboo for Bonn and its partners
- Thyssen fears takeover by Krupp
- Lowest growth since the end of the war in insurance business
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition wants to continue to support the east
- President of the Federal Employment Office Bernhard Jagoda says it is possible to halve the number of unemployed by the year 2000
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says stability of the euro is more important that the timetable
- Wolfgang Schaeuble, leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group, says that aid for reconstruction of east Germany must be kept at a high level
- Bank association presses for punctual launch of euro on 1 January, 1999
- The French government is alarmed by fusion of German BASF subsidiary Kali and the Canadian Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan (PCS)
DIE WELT

- EU ministers approve German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's euro calculations. Waigel says Germany will fulfil Maastricht criteria and that a delay in plans for European monetary union were not an issue
- Opposition SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine sceptical about an agreement on tax reform with government
- Ruling coalition wants to support east Germany. CDU proposes 10-point plan to maintain aid
- Car insurance will be more expensive this year
